newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands of Belgians protest justice system.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Belgians protest justice system.

text.p: King Albert called for profound change as tens of thousands of Belgians took to the streets on Friday to vent their anger over judicial bungling and corruption in Belgium's child sex and murder scandal.
On the fourth straight day of demonstrations, some 30,000 students swarmed through the streets of Ghent and Antwerp calling for an overhaul of the justice system.
Chanting "Gestapo", some students clashed with police who arrested 50 people.
Banners held aloft by demonstrators protested over the removal of a top investigator probing the child sex scandal saying it was part of a top-level cover-up.
In other towns traffic was halted by processions of people outraged at bungling and incompetence revealed in the case.
As Brussels braced for what one newspaper dubbed the March of the Century on Sunday in support of parents of dead and missing children, a minister warned the government could fall.

"If the government does not listen to the public and does not make sure that the investigation can continue perfectly it could fall over the Dutroux case," Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte told Nieuwe Panorama magazine.

Belgium, normally a placid corner of western Europe, has been in shock since mid-August when two young girls who had been sexually-abused were rescued from a secret dungeon in a house owned by rapist Marc Dutroux.
The bodies of four other victims missing for over a year were subsequently discovered.

"The Queen and I are convinced that this tragedy must be the occasion for a moral rebirth and a profound change in our country," Albert told a round table conference of the parents of missing children.
But the removal from the case on Monday of popular investigating magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte sparked spontaneous demonstrations and allegations of a cover-up.

Connerotte, whose job as an investigating magistrate is to build a balanced file both for and against prosecution, was ordered off the case because he attended a free spaghetti dinner given by a group helping the parents of missing children.
Public disgust has bridged the country's divide between French and Dutch-speakers.
In Brussels about 50 buses carrying symbolic white ribbons and pictures of Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo -- two of the girls found dead in August -- formed a convoy through the city.
One had a broom sticking out of the window reflecting the public demand for a sweep out of corruption.
So far 13 people have been charged in connection with the probe. A team of more than 350 police are on the case and still searching for at least seven other missing children.
Sunday's rally, which police expect to draw more than 100,000 people, many of them children, is being organised by the parents of some of the missing children.
Weekend leave has been cancelled and 400 police and 1,000 gendarmes will be on duty hoping for an uneventful rally but prepared to stamp out any incidents that may occur.
The parents of the dead and missing children appealed for calm and dignity on Sunday, a sentiment echoed by Albert and Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene.
Many of the marchers will be dressed in white and carrying white flowers as a gesture of sympathy and hope.
Belgian railways said on Friday it had already pre-sold 40,000 cut-price tickets and expected the number to double.
